utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please take the card and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith will now be asking you some questions. Mr. Moore. You keep changing on me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. My headset was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Vujic. I was born on the 27th of June, 1933 in the village of Trnakovac, Nova Gradiska municipality, Croatia. I'm an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think that actually where you were born was in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Prior to your retirement, what was your principal occupation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I worked with the security bodies of the JNA. I was in charge of unit protection and I also had to protect all the JNA institutions. For the most part, our activity was against terrorism. I worked with these bodies for a number of years, and at the end of my career I was chief of security. I was chief of the security department at the graduate military school centre in Belgrade. When I retired, my rank at retirement was colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would just like to in very general terms go through, please, your career. I say in very general terms. I think it's right to say that in 1956/1957 that you were an officer, you were ranked lieutenant, I think at that time, and you were part of what is called the Yugoslav contingent of forces in Egypt's Suez Canal area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Once I had completed my secondary education, I applied to the school for active armoured units, after which I served with the armoured units as tank commander and tank platoon commander. In 1956, I was with the guards division, their armoured units, and I was transferred to the Yugoslav forces within the UNEF, U-N-E-F, and I was posted to the Suez Canal the in Sinai Desert and in the Gaza strip. I was commander of a reconnaissance platoon, and I was the first to report to the commander of the forces, General Burns. I was commander of the honourary platoon, and I reported pursuant to orders from the platoon commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Erakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I deal principally with the fact that you stated that you were chief of security or of the security department at the graduate military school centre in Belgrade. What exactly did that involve?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: My job was to protect the institution. This institution trained officers who were to become generals later on. But they got their training to become majors and other basic ranks in the KOV, land forces academy. This centre also had a military academy training men for the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to -- I may come back to your military training in due course, but I want to move on in time, if I may. I'd like to deal, please, with the autumn of 1991, and I think it's right to say that you received a telephone call from Colonel Radovan Radivojevic. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: After the state of emergency was declared by the Yugoslav presidency as our Supreme Command, I was summoned by Colonel Radivojevic Radovan, who was the chief of one organisational unit within the security administration, and a member of the board of the security administration, Aleksander Vasiljevic. General Aleksander Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just try to keep our answers as short as possible, and then I will deal with the topic and expand it. Can we deal with it that way, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was the -- what was the purpose of his telephone call to you? What did he want you to do?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: He called me and he wanted me to agree to join an operations group or a team that was set up by the security administration. It was envisaged that this team would comprise a retired officer of the Security Services, those without a wartime assignment, as well as active duty security officers from units subordinated to Colonel Radivojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have mentioned about a team. I think you were assigned to the group. Who else, or what senior officers were assigned to that team? Can you tell the Court the names, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: This group or team was headed by Colonel Slavko Tomic, a retired colonel, Colonel Boguljub Kijanovic, Colonel Radivojevic second in command, a deputy, Captain First Class Slobodan Stosic, and several other officers from the security administration later joined the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was an officer called Kijanovic in this group or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Kijanovic was part of the group. As I have already said, he was the deputy or second in command to Colonel Radivojevic. As far as I know he retired in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the purpose of this group of senior officers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Our task, the way it was relayed to us by Colonel Radivojevic was to work in the first collection centre for prisoners of war. It was precisely at this time that this collection centre was established in a village called Begejci on a farm near Zrenjanin. This was in Zitiste municipal territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But what were you actually to do. You've told us the location, but what was the purpose of the group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the provisions of the international law of war, and provisions based on federal laws, the purpose of our group was to work with prisoners of war. We would interview them, screen them for possible crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when we talk about crimes, are we talking about war crimes or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: We're talking about war crimes, yes. My impression on arrival there was that those were prisoners of war from war-torn areas, areas affected by armed conflict. They hailed from villages in the area between Ilok and Vukovar. Paramilitary units had been organised, Croatian paramilitary units in those areas, and these units were armed by the HDZ. Crisis Staffs were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When we talk about war crimes -- I'll just stop if I may, as there may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, again, if you could just occasionally look at me to see if we can shorten the questions down, I would be -- the answers down, I would be very grateful. When we talk about war crimes, war crimes by whom upon whom?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: The prisoners were members of paramilitary units of Croatia. The crimes being screened were crimes that had been committed by paramilitary units or by individuals in the war-torn area. Likewise, we conducted interviews with these people in order to screen them for possible crimes. Also those possibly committed by JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What expertise did you have, as far as you are aware, that made you selected for this task?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: In my previous answer when I talked about my career, maybe I should have provided more detail in order for you to understand that I had spent over 30 years working with various security bodies protecting units and institutions. Over the last couple of years of my career, I acquired such experience that my superiors enlisted my assistance for such tasks as the research on terrorism against the units and institutions of the JNA. I achieved certain results in my work by uncovering illegal groups and individuals who promoted terrorism as part of their programme or philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the war crimes that you say you were investigating? What rules or laws were you to use when considering whether war crimes were being committed or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: We based our work on provisions governing the work of security bodies in the JNA we had rules on the application of the international law of war. If I remember correctly, it was published back in 1988. It was signed by the army General Veljko Kadijevic, federal secretary for All People's Defence. Further, our work was in keeping with the relevant federal laws, the federal Law on Criminal Procedure, for example. It was within this general framework that we applied a number of other positions and regulations governing the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court, in due course the Prosecution will be calling a witness called Theunens who will deal with these regulations in relation to other matters. It may well be that with this witness I will deal with small parts, but that matter will be dealt with in due course. I really don't want to go into the investigation at the collection centre. I'm quite sure my learned friends will have lots of questions about that. But I'd like to move on, if I may, about a time when you were reassigned, if I may use that phrase. I want to deal with approximately the 18th of November of 1991. Now, can I just deal, please, with what I will call your reassignment in respect of inquiries in the Vukovar area. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. And I believe that there is something else I should have said. I should have told you about how the work in the first collection centre at Begejci was organised. Colonel Tomic headed the operations team number one. I was there, too; Colonel Kijanovic was there; Slobodan Stosic was also one of the people there. This was coordinated on behalf of the security administration by Major Miroslav Zivanovic. Further, there was another team belonging to the security body of the 1st Military District. This team was headed by Major Dzukic. The camp commander or the collection centre commander, if you like, was Lieutenant-Colonel Petkovic. He was from the logistics units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I just explain that I want to deal really with questions in and around the Vukovar area. It in no way stops you in giving evidence perhaps in due course about this camp, but I want to focus about your reassignment to Vukovar. That is why you are here to give evidence, principally. Do you follow? Now, can I just ask you, please, when did you receive notification that you may have to go to the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: It was Sunday evening, as far as I remember. The 17th of November, 1991. When we came back to Belgrade over the weekend to see our families. It was on the 18th of November that we were supposed to all meet up in Belgrade, because Colonel Kijanovic was to check the vehicles, do the regular maintenance, write up receipts for the fuel. Colonel Kijanovic [as interpreted] went to get our assignments. After that we returned to Zitiste which was our base before we were off to Begejci, and that was also where Major Miroslav Zivanovic was called over the telephone by someone from the security administration instructing him for us to cease work in Begejci, to stop all activity, and that we should expect to be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica that same day because a POW camp was being set up there, the reason being that everybody was expecting Vukovar to fall. It was on that same day that we were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention in relation to the transcript. Page 45, line 9. It says: "Colonel Kijanovic went to get our assignment." I think that this involved Colonel Tomic. Let me just also say that we have many problems with the way the names are transcribed in the transcript. I'm afraid that this might become even a greater problem later on. Perhaps this witness is going too fast and the interpreters are not able to catch up all the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't know if you heard that or not. I know it's difficult sometimes to be -- slow down one's natural speed, but if you could try and keep your answers a little shorter and just slow down so that it doesn't completely disorientate you, I'm sure the interpreters would be very grateful. Now, can I just deal, then, please, with -- you said that you were going to be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica. Can we just move then, please, to what your understanding was when you -- when you got there. Why were you going to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: We were told that we would continue the assignment in the newly established POW camp. To which people would be brought from the combat area. We were told that it was our task to take these people in. There was already a major there from the security administration preparing the premises for our stay here. The camp, which was situated in Sremska Mitrovica in the KP Dom, which is a penitentiary institution, was under the jurisdiction of the ministry of justice of the SFRY, which means that it was a federal institution. It was our understanding that an agreement had been reached between relevant ministries or, as they were called at the time, federal secretariats, about the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about Vukovar and you were expecting a large number of people coming to that camp from Vukovar. Can you remember in very general terms how many people were expected?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: We were not told the figure of people. On the job we learned about this through our activities. Upon our arrival there, once the preparations for our stay were conducted, Colonel Tomic received an assignment or, rather, he was called to the telephone and told, as he later related to us, by Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, chief of security organ in Sid, in the Sid garrison, that we were requested to come to Sid as soon as possible, where we would be given our further tasks related to the evacuation of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who was in the group that went to Sid, please? Can you tell us the names of the people who went to Sid with you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: The senior officer, the chief of that group, was Colonel Slavko Tomic. We had a military vehicle with the JNA plates; Colonel Kijanovic was in charge of the vehicle. He was also Colonel Tomic's deputy. The next person was myself, Slobodan Stosic, and a warrant officer who was retired was from the Osijek garrison and was quite familiar with Vukovar. As far as I can remember, we came to Sid at around 1800 hours on the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: For completeness sake, can you remember the name of the warrant officer, or would you wish to refresh your memory from your statement, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: First class warrant officer was called Stevan Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we deal, then, please, when you got to Sid. You've told us that you were going to be given your instructions. Who gave those new instructions to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: We stopped somewhere in the centre of Sid, near the main post office building. We were told that the headquarters of Colonel Petkovic was located there. Colonel Tomic said that he would go on his own to report to Colonel Petkovic and to receive further instructions. We stayed there waiting for about 10 minutes in the car or next to the car. Colonel Tomic, upon his return, said that we would receive a combat -- or rather, we would receive an armoured vehicle to escort us, and that we would -- we were supposed to head out straight to Negoslavci where we were to report to Colonel Mrksic, commander of the Operations Group South and that we would receive our assignments from him. This is what Slavko Tomic said that he had heard from Colonel Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you then follow those instructions and go to Negoslavci and report to Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We followed the armoured vehicle, combat armoured vehicle, and reached Negoslavci at around 2000 hours, as far as I can remember. Once there we reported to Colonel Mrksic, who met with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say you reported to Colonel Mrksic. Did you see any other officers present when you reported to Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Tomic took us in, we introduced ourselves. Colonel Mrksic met with us. In addition to him, we also greeted Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic, who, at that time held the command post with Colonel Mrksic. In addition to him there was Chief of Staff of Colonel Mrksic, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, and Major Sljivancanin, Veselin, assistant of Colonel Mrksic for security matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic brief you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I understand your question to mean whether we had been informed. Yes. Colonel Mrksic informed us of the basic operation situation and, in principal, with the security situation, and the tasks that we were to be given. As far as I can remember, and based on what I stated in my statements, Colonel Mrksic first said something about the main elements concerning the guards brigade. He was the commander of that brigade. And he told us in brief terms what was generally known, that the brigade -- or rather, the brigade subordinated to him was engaged in the operations area in Vukovar and that its mission was to carry out the deblocking of the barracks to establish law and order in the area engulfed by combat operations, which could be seen as an ethnic conflict. Further, as far as I can remember, he said that from the inception of combat operations the brigade had suffered great losses through combat with paramilitary formations of Croatia, which he referred to as Ustashas. He also said that the brigade had accomplished its mission after drawn-out fighting. And that Vukovar was finally liberated. He said that all resistance had been crushed in the area of combat operations, that paramilitary units of Croatian army had surrendered in an organised fashion, that Marin Vidic, Bili, the plenipotentiary of the Croatian government and President Tudjman had asked to meet him and accepted the truce as well as accepted the surrender of Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just before we go any further, may I ask a question? Was there any mention about prisoners of war under the control of JNA forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that all resistance had been crushed, that Ustashas had surrendered, that there were cases of mass surrender, that fierce resistance had been put up in the defence area known as Mitnica, and that an agreement on surrender had been reached there as well, with certain conditions, which were put by the defence commander of that area. He said that people were leaving Vukovar en masse, women, children, the elderly, that they were being evacuated, and that they were given accommodation in the holding centre or collection centre in Velepromet. That there was no further resistance, except that the situation at the hospital was somewhat unclear. The hospital had not yet been evacuated because, based on the available information, there were numerous war criminals hiding there and that they were mingling with the wounded, the sick, and other civilians who were at the hospital. He said that Major Sljivancanin would brief us about that in detail within the implementation of the tasks, including our tasks. I apologise, in addition to that, Colonel Mrksic also said that the brigade had accomplished its mission but that it had a lot of losses. As far as I can remember, and this is what I also said in my statements, over 600 persons were put out of action. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us about Velepromet, women, children and elderly. Was there any reference to prisoners of war being held or being present at the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was mention of them. I can tell you in greater detail what Major Veselin Sljivancanin said about that, because Colonel Mrksic said that the major would brief us separately about that situation concerning the prisoners of war and that he would give us our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how long did that briefing take, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the colonel briefed us all the way up to a certain point in time when a younger officer came in and reported to him that a motor vehicle belonging to the brigade had hit a mine and that four or six persons or soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But the question that I asked, if you are able to assist us, is how long it actually took for that briefing from Colonel Mrksic to your group. If you can't say, do say.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I can't be accurate. I think that it was between 10 and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And from what you could hear from him and the situation that you were aware of, did he appear well-informed about the situation in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of us realised that the colonel was in charge of the situation and that throughout the implementation of the task he was in control, that he had units under his control, as well as the commanders of units within his area of responsibility. Perhaps I failed to mention that the colonel said that within the Operations Group South there were some other units there subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he indicate if the Velepromet facility was within his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the facility was not far from the JNA barracks, where the brigade units were located. Also, that this Velepromet facility of which I heard for the first time right then and there, I had no idea what kind of a facility it was, but we were told that it was within the area of responsibility of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we now move on, please. You have told us that Colonel Mrksic indicated to you that Major Sljivancanin would continue the briefing in relation to the task that he was going to set, "he" being Mrksic. Do you remember saying that in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection centres around the fact that I think that the witness didn't say that Mr. Sljivancanin would inform them about the tasks set out by Colonel Mrksic. I don't think that this is what the witness said. I think that my learned friend can rephrase this, otherwise it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps a misleading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In my submission, it's not a misleading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My recollection is that the -- Major Sljivancanin was to brief them in greater detail about one aspect, that is POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just read what I have on the transcript and just, if I may. "Question: You told us about Velepromet, women, children ... elderly. Was there any reference to prisoners of war being held or being present at the Velepromet facility? "Answer: Yes, there was mention of them. I can tell you in greater detail what Major Sljivancanin said about that, because Colonel Mrksic said that the major would brief us separately concerning the prisoners of war and that he would give us our tasks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that is at page 50, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think it's perhaps splitting hairs a little. But I understand that to be, in effect, what I said. You understand it differently, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I rephrase it and see exactly what the purpose is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you said that in actual fact Colonel Mrksic had said that Major Sljivancanin would brief you about the tasks, were those tasks that, as far as you're aware, Colonel Mrksic was aware, or was it just tasks that Major Sljivancanin was going to give you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that Colonel Mrksic knew what the tasks were concerning the evacuation of the prisoners of war, but that certain details concerning the plan about which Major Sljivancanin said that it existed, the evacuation plan; namely, that he would be the one who would inform us about the contents of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we then deal, please, with whether in actual fact Major Sljivancanin did give you a briefing about that? And when I say "you," I mean collectively, not just you individually.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I have omitted to say that in addition to our group there was also a group of members of security organ from the 1st Military District. At its head was Major Muncan Dragan. My understanding was that they were subordinated to Colonel Petkovic -- or rather, to General Mile Babic. They were present there as well. When Major Sljivancanin convened the meeting in order to brief us, the meeting was held in front of the command headquarters in an area next to a road. In the meantime, Major Sljivancanin left the room of the command headquarters to do some other things, and then once he returned he convened the meeting in order to brief us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough then, please, slowly, to inform the Court of what Major Sljivancanin said in that briefing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin, at the outset, gave us certain information about combat activities, enough to give us an introduction and explain how it came that Vukovar was liberated and how the surrender came about, the surrender of prisoners of war or units of Ustashas, as he called them. These are the units that they had been engaged in heavy combat with. He also said that they surrendered en masse and that the problem that remained was the evacuation of the hospital. According to his reliable sources, there were many war criminals hiding in the hospital, Ustashas who had been killing people. They were afraid to surrender and were hiding in the hospital, passing themselves off as the wounded, some of them even inflicted wounds on themselves. He said that he had taken measures to investigate the matters at the hospital, to shed light on them and that he did so by talking to the hospital director, Dr. Vesna Bosanac, to Dr. Njavro, and said that Colonel Mrksic had talked to Marin Vidic, who asked to meet with the commander, that is to say, Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin, in that briefing, make reference to the Velepromet collection centre?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I think that it was Colonel Tomic who asked Sljivancanin where Ustashas were located and how many of them there were. Major Sljivancanin replied that the -- their accurate numbers of these Ustashas who were in hiding were not known, that they were mixed up with the other people and that at Velepromet that there were women with children, that there were elderly people. And that together with them in -- on the same premises, there were prisoners of war, as well as members of the Territorial Defence. That all of them were there together, and practically one could not tell how many prisoners of war there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was it indicated at that time who was controlling the Velepromet facility, or which units were controlling the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major Sljivancanin may have said that the civilians, the refugees first tried to enter the compound of the barracks, but that they were, however, prevented from doing that and that they were then put up at Velepromet, across from the barracks. He then said that the provisional collection centre at Velepromet was secured by the police forces which were under his command, that the unit was headed by Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, and that there was a group of senior officers subordinated to him, Second Lieutenant Zvonko Cekic, and other junior officers subordinated to him, forensic officers and members of the military police who were securing the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You may have answered my question at the very end. When you referred to police subordinated to Major Sljivancanin, are you referring to civil police or military police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: No, I said units of the military police. I didn't know the strength of the unit; I didn't know how many men there were. I was told that this was a unit of the military police, which was commanded over by Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, who was subordinated to Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In very simple terms, if you could do that, what was your task at Velepromet, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin said that once the buses arrive, our task was to conduct screening of the people and separate the able-bodied men, aged 16 to 60 or 65, from women and children and that they were to be evacuated to Sremska Mitrovica. My understanding was that our task was indeed to consist of these activities. Major Sljivancanin then said that this had already been done. He said that in response to Tomic's question. He said that the screening had already been done, that the women and children and the elderly were already on the buses and were waiting to be transported to the territory of the Republic of Croatia. We were supposed to report to Captain Borisavljevic who would meet with us and brief us and that he already knew that we were to arrive there. Somebody then asked whether that same evening the hospital itself would be evacuated, and Major Sljivancanin said, as I have already indicated, that the situation was quite complex and that he was doing his best to check the identities of the persons in the hospital who was there and so on and so forth and that Dr. Vesna Bosanac had agreed to draw up a list of all those present in the hospital, the wounded, the sick, the civilians, and the hospital staff. Part of the task was also given to Dr. Njavro, as far as the hospital staff was concerned, and Marin Vidic, Bili, had to take care of the people from his -- from under his command, because Dr. Njavro had said that in the last couple of days the Crisis Staff had operated from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's a very long answer. But may I just deal with perhaps that meeting with -- at Velepromet -- that meeting a Negoslavci. When the meeting was coming to an end, was there anything that Major Sljivancanin said that surprised you or caught your attention?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Toward the end of the meeting when we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the question as it is phrased is leading. If the witness heard this on this meeting with Sljivancanin, then he should have been allowed to proceed and finish what he had to say instead of being interrupted and then asked a leading question. He was trying to describe the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lukic, but I believe the last question not to be leading. It was directing to one particular subject matter, which in the context of the generality of the answer is understandable. So, yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, can you remember what you were going to say? Would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I will follow the events as they unfolded at the time. I know that Major told us that we were to be taken to Velepromet by a lance-corporal from under his command of the military police, and that he was not going to accompany us there because he had our tasks to attend to. . As we were preparing to leave, he told us the following: Don't be surprised if you find Chetniks there slaughtering Ustashas. I was surprised by that, as were the others, I could tell that. But nobody asked what Chetniks he was talking about, because Major Sljivancanin had told us only -- had told us that members of the Territorial Defence were there, and I recall that Branko Korica who was next to me made the following comment while looking me in the eyes, "How come it was going to be the Chetniks lecturing us on slaughtering people?" We then set out toward the Velepromet building. As far as I remember, the distance is some four to five kilometres. We went on foot and moved quite quickly, we were met there by Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, who reported to us. I haven't highlighted the fact, however, that Colonel Tomic, before our departure, said that he suggested that I be the one in charge of our task at Velepromet. In his words the reason being that he was a man of an advanced age, I was his junior, and I was more familiar with these matters, both based on my knowledge, and my experience from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to deal with your meeting with Borisavljevic. Where did you meet him, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: It was during the briefing that I met Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic for the first time. He said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question I asked you was, I think, where. Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My first meeting with him was at the gate when he reported to us there. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The gate of where? The gate of where?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand, I haven't understood the interpretation. It was at the gate of Velepromet. I apologise, I have trouble hearing the interpretation. That's why I'm perhaps failing to answer your question. Before I met Srecko Borisavljevic for the first time, at the gate at the entrance to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with the briefing -- you seem to have difficulty hearing. Are you still having difficulty hearing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I can hear you well now. After a couple of days, after we had managed to get accustomed to Velepromet, I first had to make myself familiar with the buildings, the hangar and all the rest that we saw there. There were no prisoners of war, I didn't see any. There were several women there though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to try and deal with this in sequence. I suspect there's been a hearing problem and an interpretation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour this is an extremely important area. Might I ask to have a slightly earlier break than normal. I know that the Colonel has asked if he could have short breaks, and I have not done that quite deliberately because of the nature of the evidence. But on the last occasion the answer did not even remotely meet the question, and I'm concerned that there will be a mix-up and then there is the suggestion that his credibility is called into issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 20 minutes to 1.00. We're going to have one of our regular breaks now and that will give you a chance to refresh yourself, and we will resume at 20 minutes to 1.00 for about another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that there was some technical problem. Could I perhaps ask the witness if he is having difficulty in hearing, because I say we have investigated it and there were problems. Would he be kind enough to indicate to myself or to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to ask you some questions, please, about the area of evidence that we had approached before the break. Do you follow? We're talking about the Velepromet facility, and we're talking about the briefing that you had at the Velepromet facility. Do you remember that piece of evidence? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just deal, please, focus on the briefing itself. Who was present at that briefing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I told Captain Borisavljevic to gather all the commanding officers subordinated to him in the meeting room. I recall that the meeting was attended by, in addition to Colonel Tomic's group, that I led a group led by Major Muncan and commanding officers of Captain Borisavljevic. I believe some 10 to 15 senior officers were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I take it so that there is an explanation for the transcript, when we talk about commanding officers of Captain Borisavljevic, you're talking about, what in the British army would be called non-commissioned officers, or officers below the Captain himself. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Under the system arrangement in the JNA, non-commissioned officers are called junior officers. These are ranks from the basic rank of sergeant up to warrant officer first class. That's the range covering junior officers. They were subordinated to Captain First Class Borisavljevic or to Second Lieutenant Zvonimir Cekic, if he was the commander of the department of forensic officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reason I asked the question is so that you understand, is your reply is as follows: "I told the captain to gather together all the commanding officers subordinated to him in the meeting room." Who -- how do we rank this phrase of commanding officers? In the British army, commanding officer are usually senior officers. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Under the system in the Yugoslav People's Army, senior officers were those from the rank of major up, whereas junior officers were those starting from second lieutenant up to captain first class. That is why all the officers who were members of the unit led by commander who was commander of a company, Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, he was their commander. I considered him their commander and they were subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, that's very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, does the term subordinate commander assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I would hope it assists, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is, as we have understood, what is being said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the phrase of command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Commanding officer is ambiguous. In English, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I believe that is clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a commanding officer of the police unit there and his subordinate commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Commanders. Of whom some 10 to 15 attending a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, and it's military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that's been made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we then just deal, please, with what was said at this particular meeting then?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I am ready to proceed telling you about the contents of the meeting, the subjects discussed. I told you that the group, which included myself, was a group of officers from the security administration. The task of which was, together with the military police, to board prisoners of war on to buses as soon as they arrive, and they were to be evacuated to the Sremska Mitrovica camp. I also indicated that we were supposed to accomplish this mission on behalf of the chief of -- of the security administration and on behalf of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you told how many people were actually at that facility, in approximate numbers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I asked Captain Borisavljevic how many prisoners of war were to be found there and he told me that they didn't know. When I told him that we were tasked with separating them, singling them out from the civilians who were there, Major Sljivancanin had told us that there were civilians there. In response to my question, Borisavljevic told me that it had already been done and that the prisoners of war had been already taken to a separate area designated for the POWs and that the military police was guarding them. Furthermore, I emphasised that our task was that we do so as soon as the buses arrive. The reason I said that was that while I was telling them what our task was, the door to the room where we had the meeting opened, it was -- rather, it was ajar, and you could see heads, bearded heads wearing cockades, as they call them, or the patch worn by the unit that I later heard styled themselves as Chetniks started appearing. In addition to them, another person wearing a MUP uniform was poking his head through the door, and I can't -- asked Captain Borisavljevic and those present there who those people were. Borisavljevic told me that they were members of the Territorial Defence and that they were there guarding prisoners of war as well. I was surprised by -- to hear that because they did not really enter the meeting room; rather, they were simply leaning into the room through the door and heckling at us, We are not going to let any buses arrive here or for them to go to Sremska Mitrovica, so on and so forth. I could hear their comments through the door. This was deliberately done by them because they wanted to show that they objected to the evacuation of the POWs and that they were not going to allow that to happen. I repeated what our task was, and I said that on behalf of the Supreme Command and the top military leadership and on behalf of the chief of the security administration, our task was that as soon as the buses arrive, we board POWs on them as soon as possible and evacuate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. So who did you repeat your -- the aims of your task? To whom did you repeat that phrase to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I repeated those words to the commanding officers present at the meeting and to those who were heckling from outside the room and saying that they disagreed with what we were preparing to do. This was therefore meant for those members of the TO and the Chetniks. I apologise. Moreover, I said that -- or rather, I asked Captain Borisavljevic whether there were any lists and whether they knew how many prisoners of war there were. He told me that there were none and that they don't know how many there were. Whereupon I said that one or two commanders should be placed in charge of every bus and that they should have two members of the military police each and that they should be responsible for the POWs and that they are boarded on the buses. I also said that, where possible, they should take note of the registration plates of every bus and to draw up lists of POWs who had -- who boarded the buses, including their names. I had a book -- a notebook with me where I noted down the names of the commanding officers who were responsible for reporting to me back after they had accomplished their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know it's a long time ago, can you remember any of the names of the people that -- or the commanders that you believed should be reporting back to you? If you can't remember, do say so.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I do remember. It was Colonel Tomic who took responsibility, as well as Colonel Kijanovic, and Captain Borisavljevic. Responsibility was also taken for this by Lieutenant-Colonel -- Second Lieutenant Cekic, as well as junior officers subordinated to both Cekic and Borisavljevic. Some other people who took charge of this included warrant officer first class Branko Korica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you keep lists of names or were you aware of the names of people who were to report back to you? Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I did that because in a way I felt that the mission might be obstructed. I felt that based on those people appearing in the corridor, whose intentions were pretty much clear, they kept saying things like, "What sort of camp are you talking about? What sort of Mitrovica are you talking about? These people aren't going anywhere." I wanted to act in a soldierly fashion. I wanted to make sure that the mission was accomplished, and that is why I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did the time come that you eventually left that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Once the meeting ended, there was a proposal by Captain Borisavljevic. He said that we should go and visit the rooms where the POWs were being held. That was how the meeting ended. And we were off to visit those rooms. Within the Velepromet compound there was not a single woman left, because all the women had already been taken away on buses. We first went to an area, or a room, when we came there, I was surprised to notice that just outside the room there were twice as many guards as we would have expected. When I say "twice as many guards," I should perhaps first say that I noticed three bearded persons outside the room wearing chapka caps with Chetnik insignia, tall, fur caps. They were carrying machine-guns. They were very tall, as compared to me, tall and well-built. And they were facing -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do continue. Do continue, Colonel, but I want to return to a piece of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: There were two stout-looking military police officers standing next to them, and those were also armed with machine-guns. They were quarreling and hassling each other. The Chetniks there refused to allow me to go into the room and have a look. The room had a tin door and a grid over it. The grid had some blinds. I tried to get nearer the room, together with Second Lieutenant Cekic, and his military police escort, but the Chetniks stood in my way and kept me from having a look. At this point I ordered Cekic to create conditions for me to go in and have a look to see who was there in the room. Once he pulled the blinds apart, the heads of the POWs who were inside emerged. I realised that they were injured, that they had head injuries. Their faces were bleeding, and some of the injuries appeared to be severe ones. I was wondering who those people were, as Marko Crevar appeared, accompanied by Count Topola. That was at least how those two persons introduced themselves. Captain Borisavljevic said that these people were TO, that these people were members of the TO staff. That they had set up their own guards in front of that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just before we go any further, you said that you were surprised initially to see twice as many guards on the door as you would normally expect. Who or what units were guarding that door, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: As I have indicated, those people were Chetniks. I was to find out later that they were subordinated to the officer who introduced himself as Vojvoda Topola. He didn't say, "I command these people" or anything like that. "These are my soldiers," anything at all to that effect. The military police officers belonged to the military police unit under Captain Borisavljevic, and Second Lieutenant Cekic. I saw three Chetniks outside the room and two military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. That, I hope, clears that issue up. Can we then just deal, please, with -- you've told us that you saw prisoners of war inside, POWs inside. They had bleeding faces, and you have told us that they were being guarded. Can you please now tell us what happened next in relation to those POWs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for forgetting something. I asked Captain Borisavljevic, "Who shut these people up in here?" And he said that this had been done by Marko Crevar, a member of the TO staff who later introduced himself as chief of the wartime S-U-P, SUP, of Vukovar, the Serb faction. I never asked how long those people had been detained there for, but I later found out that Marko Crevar was proceeding against those people. At least that was my understanding at the time and I am about to explain this in my further testimony. After that, I continued to visit the remaining areas where the prisoners of war were being held. And in some of the rooms, and this is what had been reported to me, I found that there were between 30 and 40 persons. While in a hangar that I entered, I was deeply affected by what I saw. Why? Because there was a large number of POWs there in that hangar. There were benches, or rather chairs with candles burning on top of them. Makeshift candles. Makeshift candles made of rope. Those prisoners of war were in the middle of their evening prayer. And they were praying out loud, "Hail, Mary," and so on and so forth. I was trying to be patient. I was trying to give them a chance to end their prayer, but they just went on regardless. And at one point I spoke up, "Who is the most senior person here? I expect the senior person to report to me right now." It was dark inside, and you could only see the outlines of human bodies in the candlelight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we go to that particular area, I want to go back to the room that was guarded, double guards and a door and you said you were able to see inside. Now, can you please focus on that piece of evidence? Were you able, or did you ever attempt to go inside that room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: I didn't go inside that room eventually. What happened was Second Lieutenant Cekic opened that blind for me, which was part of the tin door. And I peered inside and saw people inside who were gasping for air as soon as the hatch opened and trying to pop their heads out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone about trying to get into that room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't try to get in. Even my chances would have been very uncertain. And I didn't know exactly how many POWs were inside, but I saw that the room was packed. And they were packed like sardines. It would have been dangerous for me to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let us then move back to where you were in relation to going into the hangar and seeing people in prayer and who was the most senior person there. Can we just deal with that area? Was there any reply when you asked about who was the most senior?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the second time I called out for the most senior person to respond, or for the commander to respond, a man walked past the chairs inside and approached me. He was a tall fighter. He must have been about 190 centimetres tall, walking in a soldierly fashion, doing the military step all the way up to me, and then he reported. He said he was the commander of that particular unit. He said his last name. He said his name was Commander Maric. He said he was the chaplain. That was when I asked him about his rank. That was all he said. He said, "I am a commander. I am Commander Maric, and I am the chaplain." I asked him how many of his soldiers were there, and he said that there were about 100 of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see the buses at any time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: The buses were not there at this point. They had not yet arrived, so I continued to tour some of the other rooms. I reached a room, or rather was brought to this room by Captain Borisavljevic and by Cekic. The rest of the people followed -- the rest of my people followed. There was a long table inside that room with a white table-cloth on top. There were medical instruments placed along that table, surgical instruments. There was a person who reported to me. This person said he was a medical doctor, and he said that he led or headed the first aid unit there. He said what his name was, but I didn't memorise it. I did have to understand, as I have indicated in all of my statements, that he was an ethnic Croat. I asked him about his mission and what he was doing there, and he said that he was told to be there by someone, Crevar or perhaps someone else. He said he was aiding the wounded. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm just trying to break it up in pieces, if I can, so it is easier to follow. You've told us that the buses hadn't arrived by that time, but do you remember the buses arriving?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the buses arrived. Captain Borisavljevic and his officers told us, "The buses are here. Colonel, sir, the buses have arrived." What they meant is that the buses had arrived outside the compound. They were waiting outside in the streets, outside the Velepromet compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were aware of the buses, did you see anything happening with regard to those prisoners of war that caught your attention?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time. I hadn't made any special observations that would have caught my attention or led me to think that anything in particular had occurred or that particular words had been spoken. I said that the buses should enter the barracks, or rather the Velepromet compound, and that they should prepare for the POWs to start boarding the buses. Back at the meeting, I had given a clear order to the effect that military discipline and order were to be strictly observed, as well as safety measures. I said that during the boarding special attention was to be paid to both the officers and the JNA officers, but also to the prisoners of war. There were several of those buses there, perhaps four or five, that managed to get inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you please -- can we please now focus on the boarding of the buses? So how did that start? Can you tell us, please, and then what occurred?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Each of the commanding officers who were told to take a group of POWs each on to the buses did as ordered, did as I had ordered them to do, and Captain Borisavljevic, too. However, at this time as the boarding was still underway, I was first approached by Warrant Officer Second Class Branko Korica. He warned me that he had heard the aforementioned Marko Crevar and Vojvoda Topola saying that they might perhaps allow for part of the POWs to be boarded on the buses and for the POWs and the buses to be evacuated. But those prisoners of war who were inside the room that I described as having twice as many guards as normal outside would not be allowed to leave. They -- he told me that they had made threats against my life, saying things like, "That colonel should be killed along with the Ustashas." This same threat was also relayed to me by Colonel Kijanovic and by Slobodan Stosic, Captain First Class Slobodan Stosic. We agreed that the buses should be allowed to leave the compound as soon as possible in order to join the column outside that had been formed. The last step to be taken was to vacate the room holding the prisoners of war, the room that I have described. I am about to explain this in the continuation of my testimony. I am about to describe this event as I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, do so, then, Colonel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: The number of TO people in the area, meaning the Chetniks, had increased, those who were outside the room. I don't know where Marko Crevar and Vojvoda Topola had brought them from, and at this point in time, once threats had been made by Crevar, who said, "Colonel, all of these people are Ustashas and criminals. They are thugs who were killing Serbs and slitting the throats of Serbs. I am already in the process of taking steps against these people, and they must be called to account for their actions. We shall not allow you to take these people away." I spoke up in order to reiterate the following: "On behalf of the Supreme Command staff, on behalf of the topmost military leadership, on behalf of the chief of the security administration, I must tell you that these are prisoners of war and they must be evacuated and taken to the Sremska Mitrovica camp." Crevar again said that these people were Ustashas, that they were criminals, and that he would not allow for these people to be taken away, even that meant having to use force or, rather, weapons, against my person or the other JNA officers present. At this point, I yet again repeated what I told him before. It was a highly unpleasant situation. This is what I said at first, "These people may have been Ustashas while they were still firing at you. But as soon as they had surrendered their weapons, as soon as they came out with their hands up, they ceased being Ustashas and became prisoners of war, from that very moment on." There was a harsh verbal clash that ensued between us. And at this point in time I was approached by Colonel Slavko Tomic and Colonel Janovic [as interpreted]. They said that they would have no part in this anymore, that they wanted no part in this mission. They also said something else. They said they were on their way to see Colonel Mrksic to inform him about what was going on. This was another thing that surprised me, because there was a bus there already for the POWs from that room to board. And I came very close to not accomplishing my mission and not carrying out my assignment. The first thing I said, I swore at one of those people. I'm really sorry, I apologise. I don't think I can use the word here, the word that I used when I swore at one of my colleagues there. In short, I asked them if they knew what they were doing, and I yelled at them. I said, "You just go and do what you must, but I will carry out my task even if it costs me my life."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with the prisoners of war themselves? We will come back and deal with your disagreement with Tomic, and I thought it was Kijanovic. But can we deal with the prisoners of war that you have informed us were not going to be released to you. Did you do anything to ensure that they would be released and placed on the buses?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: There were military police commanding officers present there, Second Lieutenant Cekic and some junior officers subordinated to him, as well as Captain Borisavljevic. I yelled out loud, "Captain Borisavljevic, report to me immediately, Captain Borisavljevic." I repeated that twice very loudly, and my words were heard throughout the compound. One of the Second Lieutenant Cekic's juniors responded, "He is not around, Borisavljevic is not around." I asked, "Where is he?" And they didn't know his whereabouts. And then I ordered loudly to Second Lieutenant Cekic that one of the officers should immediately be sent to Colonel Mrksic to tell him briefly about the situation that had occurred at Velepromet and to tell him that I was requesting a reinforcement from the military police. One of the officers, it was either Cekic or one of his junior officers said, "Colonel, sir, there's a BOV here. It's an APC belonging to the military police, an armoured personnel carrier. This is in case force is ever used against you, you should use it to overcome any resistance. And it's in order to re-establish military law and order," or public law and order as civilians say. I then ordered for that APC to be brought inside the compound to drive up as close as possible to that room with POWs inside, those who had been described as Ustashas and criminals. Once I had that vehicle in an appropriate position, a position allowing me to carry out my task, I ordered an officer or a junior officer who was the crew commander, he was up in the turret, to introduce himself, which he did. I said right there in front of everybody that I was taking over command and that the room was to be emptied and that the people from the room were to be taken on to those buses -- or rather, on to that bus. I issued an order that he should charge the machine-gun on his turret and to train it on me, Second Lieutenant Cekic and others who were in charge of evacuating the room. I also issued a loud command which meant that I was prepared to lay down my life in order to accomplish my mission. I said to the junior officer on the turret that he should train the machine-gun on me, my movements and that of Second Lieutenant Cekic. And that if I were to issue a command he should start firing in the direction in which I ordered, and if needed, fire at me as well. After issuing this command, I ordered Second Lieutenant Cekic to empty the room, to evacuate it, and to board the prisoners of war on to buses. This is what we did. We literally - I mean by this Cekic, two or three soldiers and policemen and some other junior officers and I - evacuated this room, sometimes taking out one prisoner of war at a time or two, in cases where they were tied to each other, and taking them to the buses. As far as I was able to see, Marko Crevar, Topola, and the Chetniks were in the vicinity, following everything that was going on. However, after the order that I issued, after the threat uttered by me, they decided not to obstruct the taking out of the prisoners of war. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. Thank you very much. Again, there is a lot of material there. I would just like to deal with the prisoners of war that you took out of the room and put into the bus. What was their physical condition when you brought them out?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: These people had serious injuries on their faces and bodies. They were bloody. Some of them were missing some parts of their bodies. They were missing ears or they had cuts on their noses. This is what I remember; this is the picture that I have. When I entered a bus, because I personally wanted to establish the figures and write down into the notebook that I had at least some names of these people, I started calling them out, asking them about their names, asking them to give me their full names. And then after a certain period of time Vojvoda Topola came inside a bus with a knife at the ready, a curved knife. And since he was quite taller than I was, I came maybe up to his beard or up to his chin, he lifted me up with both hands up in the air and then put this knife right below my neck and started yelling, "Hey, old man, you won't manage to take these Ustashas and criminals out. They have to pay for what they did to the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When he did that to you, how did you react to him? Did you do anything to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I used the terms that he was familiar with. I told him, "Come to your senses, Vojvoda," which means that I urged him to think about his acts, because his acts would have certain consequences. Then we started a scuffle, and he was trying to reach out with his arms and hurt some prisoners. He was waving around with his knife or his dagger towards them. I told him several times, "Come to your senses, Vojvoda. What you're doing is detrimental to the Serb people." I took out my pistol and I held it up against his stomach. This shoving of ours on the bus lasted for quite a while until Second Lieutenant Cekic issued a stern warning, came with two policemen and dragged Vojvoda Topola out of the bus. Throughout that time, while this was unfolding on the bus, the driver of the bus who wore a JNA uniform would occasionally turn back or sort of half turn, and it was obvious that he felt quite uncomfortable. He didn't know how to help in that situation. And as he was turning around, I recognised him, but I didn't ask him to help me. At any rate, I am prepared to invite -- or rather, I was prepared to invite Lieutenant Cekic and other policemen to tell them that we should all go in that bus with Vojvoda Topola to the command headquarters of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The people, the prisoners of war that were taken from that room and placed into the bus, did you take any of the names or can you remember any of the names of the people who were removed from the room and then placed on the bus?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I managed to jot down some names in my notebook. I remember some of the names that were known to me then and that I gave in my statements given before the military court or to The Hague investigators, or to the court in Belgrade. I can now remember only that there were sometimes two persons with the same last name. This is how I still remember the last name Molnar. I remember the last name Dosen, Hodak. Perhaps some others as well, but I'm not fully certain, so I think that this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. What then happened to the -- the bus itself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: The bus escorted by the armoured combat vehicle, Lieutenant Cekic and his policemen or soldiers made it possible for the bus to leave the compound, but it was only then that the armoured combat vehicle made a turn and started following the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about certain names that you remembered. One was Molnar and another one Dosen.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, these are the last names that I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the people who were in that bus or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: It wasn't until many years later, that is to say 1998, at a funeral of a colleague of mine, a colonel, where a number of officers assembled, either retired ones or active-duty ones, that my former superior commander, Colonel Bane Modosan came up to me. He was also superior commander to Slavko Tomic and Bogoljub Kijanovic. As the coffin left to the chapel, he came up to me, took me by my arm and started talking to me. He said, "Was it possible for a bus to be kidnapped?" He knew that I was there on a mission. He probably heard this from Colonel Tomic as well. And he said that the driver of that bus, Mihajlo Vukic, or, as we used to call him, Maestro Mile, told him in confidence that he had experienced a very unpleasant situation when he was met by a group of armed persons who boarded his bus and ordered him to take the bus to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In relation to the bus itself, did you actually follow the bus that evening, the bus with the prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't my task, actually. Major Sljivancanin told me that there was there was an evacuation plan, there was a unit which was supposed to escort the buses, which is to say that all measures had been envisioned within the plan aimed at completing the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. It's actually probably evidentially an appropriate moment, and unless the Court wishes me to continue, I would respectfully submit that might be a good time to adjourn today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. We have gone a minute over. We must adjourn now for the day, as another trial carries on here. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, if you would be good enough to return then. Thank you. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
